newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi suspect gives U.S. best lead in bomb probe.
newsitem.headline: Saudi suspect gives U.S. best lead in bomb probe.

text.p: The deportation to the United States of a suspect in a bombing that killed Americans in Saudi Arabia gives Washington investigators their best lead yet after a year of frustration, Gulf analysts said on Wednesday.

Twelve months after a fuel truck packed with explosives killed 19 U.S. airmen in the kingdom, the United States is still pleading with Saudi rulers for more cooperation and has not been able to interview any witnesses or suspects.
Suspect Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh was flown under Canadian and FBI guard to Washington from prison in Ottawa on Tuesday.

"This is the breakthrough the Americans have been waiting for," said one Saudi-based Western analyst. "They've been frustrated every step of the way by the Saudis' refusal to hand over any of their evidence."

Canadian court documents identified Sayegh, 29, a Saudi Shi'ite Moslem, as the driver of a car that gave the go-ahead signal for the bomb-laden truck involved in the June 25 attack, which also wounded hundreds of U.S. servicemen.
They said he belonged to the radical Saudi Hizbollah (Party of God). Sayegh has denied involvement in the attack but sources close to him said he may know others who were involved.
The U.S. Justice Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, which has been probing the blast at Saudi Arabia's oil capital Dhahran, have complained often and loudly about lack of Saudi help.

The FBI has criticised the kingdom for frustrating U.S. efforts to determine responsibility for the attack and FBI officials privately complained that their agents were not permitted to question Saudi citizens, were not told about arrests, and that Saudi authorities refused to share all their evidence with them.
The FBI has been waiting to interrogate Sayegh since his arrest in Canada in March, believing he may have important information about those responsible for the bombing.

U.S. officials have been seeking independent verification of Saudi allegations that Iran, branded by Washington as a sponsor of international "terrorism", was behind the attack -- a charge denied by Iran's Shi'ite rulers.
A U.S. official told a Senate hearing in Washington in April the United States had not concluded that Iran was behind the attack but would take "appropriate action" if it did.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen made the latest plea for Saudi cooperation on Sunday during a visit to the kingdom.

He told reporters after a meeting in Jeddah with King Fahd's heir apparent Prince Abdullah and Defence Minister Prince Sultan that Prince Abdullah indicated "full cooperation would be given" in the still incomplete investigation.
Cohen said he "reiterated what President (Bill) Clinton had said, that we expect full cooperation and we expect we will receive it".
U.S. officials in Washington said Sayegh would make an initial court appearance before a federal judge on Wednesday.

As part of a sealed plea deal he would admit at another hearing on Thursday to lesser conspiracy charges involving an unrelated attack against the United States that was plotted in the Middle East but never carried out, they said.

Sayegh would cooperate with U.S. authorities and tell them what he knew about the bombing at Khobar Towers, a housing complex for thousands of U.S. airmen stationed in Saudi Arabia to enforce the Clinton Administration's "dual containment" policy against Iran and Iraq.
The Pentagon reviewed U.S. force protection in the Gulf after the blast and transferred thousands of airmen to a remote airbase in the desert 90 miles (145 km) south of Riyadh.
Sayegh's lawyer said his client feared he would be executed if he had been sent back to Saudi Arabia, where his wife and two daughters still live.

Four Saudi suspects in a bombing at a military training centre in the Saudi capital Riyadh in November 1995 that killed five American servicemen and two Indians were beheaded before U.S. investigators were given a chance to question them.
Another suspect wanted by U.S. and Saudi authorities for the two bombings, exiled dissident Osama bin Laden, remains free.

Bin Laden, identified by the U.S. State Department as a major world sponsor of Islamic extremism, has denied involvement in the blasts but vowed to wage jihad or holy war against U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia because of American support of Israel.
